market_context: United States and Canada; safe home refrigeration of cooked fish and seafood.
title: How Long Does Cooked Fish Last in the Fridge?

seo.title: How Long Cooked Fish Lasts in the Fridge
seo.meta_description: Cooked fish and seafood generally keep 3–4 days in a refrigerator at 40 °F or below. Learn when the clock starts and when to throw leftovers out.
seo.search_intent: Determine how many days cooked fish can be refrigerated safely and how to store leftovers correctly.

excerpt: Cooked fish and seafood generally keep for 3 to 4 days in a refrigerator at 40 °F or below. Count from the day the food was cooked, not from when you moved it to a new container. If it sat out too long or you are unsure how long it has been stored, discard it.
content_html:
Cooked fish can look perfectly fine on day three and still leave you wondering whether dinner is pushing its luck. The most useful answer comes from time and temperature, not a smell test: cooked fish and seafood are generally best treated as 3- to 4-day refrigerator leftovers when kept at 40 °F (4.4 °C) or below.

That is the storage window used by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service. It is not a magic moment when fish suddenly changes on day five. It is a practical safety limit for refrigerated leftovers.

Count from the day it was cooked

If you cooked salmon Monday night, Monday is the start of the storage story. Moving it into a different container Tuesday does not restart the clock.

A small date label on the container works better than relying on memory, especially when several leftovers are in the refrigerator at once.

Prompt refrigeration matters as much as the number of days

The 3- to 4-day guidance assumes the fish was chilled promptly. Perishable food should not spend long stretches at room temperature; the usual rule is no more than about two hours, and less in very hot conditions.

You do not need to leave a large pan on the counter until it is completely cold. Dividing food into shallow containers helps it cool more quickly in the refrigerator.

Keep it covered and in a reliably cold part of the fridge

Store cooked fish in a clean, covered container. That limits drying, keeps odors contained, and reduces contact with other foods.

The refrigerator door experiences larger temperature swings than an interior shelf, so leftovers are better kept inside the main compartment. If you are unsure about actual refrigerator temperature, an inexpensive appliance thermometer is more useful than guessing from the control dial.

Smell can tell you when to reject food, but not when it is safe

A sour odor, obvious slime, or major texture change is enough reason to throw fish away. The reverse is not reliable: food that smells normal can still contain harmful bacteria.

That is why a five-day-old container does not become safe because it passes a sniff test. Use the time-and-temperature history as the decision rule.

Fish in pasta, rice, or sauce does not get a new clock

Adding cooked fish to a casserole or sauce does not reset its storage age. Treat the completed dish as a perishable leftover and keep track of when its ingredients were prepared.

Likewise, reheating an older leftover does not automatically give it another four days. Heat can make dinner pleasant again; it does not erase an uncertain storage history.

Freeze it before you reach the edge of the window

If you know you will not eat the fish within a few days, freeze it while it is still safely refrigerated. USDA guidance lists about three months as a good-quality target for cooked fish in the freezer.

Freezing is preservation, not rescue. Do not freeze fish that has already spent too long warm or that has exceeded a safe refrigerated storage window and expect the freezer to make it safe again.

Reheat only what you plan to eat

Repeatedly warming and cooling the entire container hurts quality and creates more time outside refrigeration. Portion out what you need and leave the rest cold.

If today is day four and you are deciding between eating the fish tonight or saving it until tomorrow, tonight is the better choice. If you will not use it, discard it.

The easy number to remember is 3–4 days, but the real protection is a continuous cold chain. Fish that was chilled promptly and held at 40 °F or below has a very different history from fish that sat on the table for hours before being refrigerated.

faq.question: Can I eat cooked fish after 5 days?
faq.answer: The standard refrigerated guidance is 3–4 days at 40 °F or below. At day five, discarding it is the safer choice even if it smells normal.

faq.question: How long does cooked salmon last in the fridge?
faq.answer: Cooked salmon follows the same general 3–4 day refrigerated window when it was chilled promptly and kept cold.

faq.question: Can I freeze cooked fish on day three?
faq.answer: Yes, provided it has been continuously refrigerated and is still within the safe storage window. Freezing earlier is better for quality.

faq.question: How can I tell if cooked fish has gone bad?
faq.answer: Off odors, slime, or obvious deterioration mean it should be discarded, but the absence of those signs does not prove safety. Time and temperature still matter.
